transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, I came in because I had to get a physical for my insurance recently, and the doctor doing it told me my weight was too low. 

Honestly, I don't really see it as an issue. To me, I just look lean. I'm a painter, so I'm up and down ladders all the time and working pretty long days, so it makes sense that I'd be trim. But they made a big deal out of it and told me I needed to come see someone, so here I am.
Over the past few months, have you been deliberately trying to eat less or restrict what you eat?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm deliberately trying to restrict, but I do keep things pretty light. Most days I just stick to coffee, and... maybe I'll have a protein bar between paint jobs. Then I'll just have a small dinner later on. Eating a full meal during the day just feels like it would slow me down, so I avoid it. It's just more practical for how I work.
When you think about eating more food or gaining weight, how does that make you feel? Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, I guess I don't really like the idea of it. If I have to eat more, like if I'm at a client dinner or I end up eating something heavy with bread, and I see the scale go up even just a little bit the next morning... I do get pretty tense. I'll usually start cutting back right away the next day just to make sure it doesn't stick. So, yeah, I suppose I do worry about putting on extra weight.
When you do eat more than usual or eat something you're worried about, do you do anything to try to counteract it — like exercising excessively, using laxatives, or making yourself vomit?

No, I don't do any of that. I've never made myself throw up or taken laxatives, or anything. And I don't really work out... my job keeps me moving enough as it is with the ladders and everything. 

If I feel like I ate too much, I just cut back on what I eat the next day, like I mentioned. But no, I don't do any of those other things you asked about.
Can you tell me your current height and weight? And roughly how much did you weigh a year ago, or at your normal adult weight before things became like this?

I'm about 5'10". As for my weight... honestly, I'm not really sure about the exact numbers. 

I know I mentioned checking the scale, but I mostly just look at it to make sure it hasn't gone up from the day before, if that makes sense. I don't really focus on the actual total number. And as for a year ago... I really have no idea. I wasn't weighing myself or paying attention to it back then. I just know I'm lighter now than I used to be, but I couldn't give you a specific starting weight or even my exact weight today.

I understand you don't focus on the exact number, but could you try to estimate your current weight as best you can? Even a rough guess would help me understand whether your weight loss might be medically significant.

I really couldn't give you a number. Like I said, I just look to see if the needle moved up from the day before. I don't look at the actual number. I know my clothes are looser, and I have to tighten my belt more, but I honestly don't know what I weigh right now.

I know the exact number isn't something you focus on, but would you be willing to step on a scale here in my office so we can get your actual weight? That will help me better understand what's going on medically.

Yeah, I can do that. If you need it for your medical records or whatever, that's fine. I just... I'd really rather not look at the number myself, if that's okay with you. You can weigh me, but I just don't want to hear what it is.

When you step on the scale here, I'll record your weight and height to calculate your BMI. But before we do that, can you tell me approximately how many pounds you think you've lost over the past year or so? Even a rough estimate — like 10 pounds, 20 pounds, 30 pounds — would help me get a sense of the timeline.

I honestly couldn't give you a good guess. Um... like I was saying, I never really weighed myself back then, so I don't know what my starting point even was. 

I couldn't tell you if it's 15 pounds or 30 pounds. I just... I don't know the difference. I just know my work pants are practically falling off me now, but as for an actual number of pounds lost, I really don't have one to give you.
Alright, let's go ahead and get you weighed and measured now. I'll record those numbers for my records.
Okay. Just point me to where the scale is. And, um... just remember, please don't say the number out loud. I'll just step on and face the wall until you've got what you need.

Thank you for being willing to step on the scale. Let me get your measurements now. [After weighing and measuring] Based on your height and weight, your BMI is [X]. For context, a BMI below 17 is generally considered significantly low. Does that align with how you've been feeling physically — any dizziness, fatigue, or cold sensitivity lately?

Um, no, not really. I haven't noticed any of that. I mean, I'm a painter, so I'm on my feet working all day, so I get tired sometimes, but it just feels like normal tiredness from work, you know? I haven't had any dizziness or... or felt unusually cold or anything like that. Physically, I feel pretty normal, to be honest.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets criteria for Anorexia Nervosa, restricting type (F50.01). She demonstrates: (1) significant weight loss with BMI in the significantly low range (<17), (2) deliberate dietary restriction (coffee and protein bar most days, avoiding full meals), (3) intense fear of weight gain (anxiety when scale increases, immediate compensatory restriction), (4) distorted body image perception (views herself as 'lean' despite medical concern), and (5) absence of binge-eating/purging behaviors, qualifying for the restricting subtype. The denial of exact weight/numbers and reluctance to hear her weight, combined with continued restrictive eating despite acknowledged weight loss, further support the diagnosis.
